source.title: A large-scale evaluation of commonsense knowledge in humans and large language models
source.authors: Tuan Dung Nguyen; Duncan J. Watts; Mark E. Whiting

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether model size relates to an evaluated capability, using commonsensicality scores rather than held-out pretraining loss. It does not reproduce the original loss-scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure pretraining loss, training tokens, training compute, or compute-optimal allocations. Its own size analysis measures commonsensicality on a survey task; this bears on V6, not V1–V5 or V7. It also reports correlations between commonsensicality and LMArena/OpenBookQA scores, recorded as related findings but not tests of V6’s scale-or-pretraining-loss relationship.
record.test_reason: The study regresses a new downstream measure, survey-based commonsensicality, on log parameter count across 23 existing instruction-tuned models from six families. That is a new-setting result on V6's scale-to-downstream relationship. It does not train models, measure pretraining loss, or fit power laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are untouched.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report a positive average association between size and commonsensicality (+8.6 points per 10× size), strongest in Flan-T5 and weakest in Mistral. They note that training-data quantity and quality likely matter, and that LLaMA-2 does not follow the pattern. Their headline conclusion is that most LLMs fall below the human median, and that smaller open-weight models can match or beat larger proprietary frontier models.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates existing instruction-finetuned models on human-survey commonsensicality and relates scores to parameter count; it does not train a controlled size/token/compute sweep or measure held-out loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that commonsensicality varies with statement features; nearly all models score higher on fact or physical-world subsets. Model-family patterns in the size association also differ.

fits_no_version.finding: Commonsensicality was not significantly correlated with LMArena Elo (r=.22, p=.31) or with OpenBookQA accuracy (r=.28, p=.21).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Survey-based commonsensicality does not track general capability benchmarks across models.

record.problems: The size analysis is observational across existing models and families, so size is entangled with training data and other model differences. It evaluates commonsensicality rather than held-out pretraining loss and covers only six families in the reported size regression.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested size-to-commonsensicality relationship were left out. Other model scores in Table C.1 were not entered as individual rows because the paper does not analyze their relationship to size in that table’s main comparison; LMArena and OpenBookQA correlations are included as related findings with versions ["none"].

untested.parts: All of it: no pretraining loss or controlled size, token or compute sweep.
All of it: no fits on small runs extrapolated to larger ones.
All of it: no compute-optimal allocation.
All of it: no shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
All of it: text-only, existing models.

The link to pretraining loss. Out-of-sample prediction of larger models' scores. Controlled scaling with data held fixed: size is confounded with training data and family. Frontier closed models of unknown size are excluded from the regression.
All of it: no exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Population-level fidelity: correlation of statement commonsensicality with humans across sizes. In Falcon it rises with size (.19 → .37 → .43 for 7B/40B/180B), but the opposite holds for Mistral and GPT families. Larger closed frontier models are not more competitive than small open models.
missing.locator: Figure 4A and text, Correlation in Statement Commonsensicality between Humans and Silicon Samples

missing.what: Cross-family size comparisons: Flan-T5-XXL (11B) ranks above Falcon-180B on human win rate despite being about 16× smaller.

record.verdict_notes: Observational across released, instruction-tuned models. Size is confounded with data, training recipe and post-training, and MoE sizes are total parameters. The measure is agreement with a human-majority survey label, not accuracy on a ground truth. The study cites Kaplan et al. only to frame the analysis and is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law behavior and bottleneck conditions.
Fitting loss curves on small runs and predicting loss for larger runs.
Fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens and its trend with compute.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling laws in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests a commonsensicality evaluation against model size, but not held-out pretraining loss, other downstream task families generally, or prediction across training runs.
Loss-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, curve fitting choices, and departures from fitted loss power laws.

relationships.condition: Pooled mixed-effects regression over 23 models in 6 families (log10 size, family random effect)
relationships.reason: Each ten-fold size increase is associated with +8.6 points commonsensicality (95% CI 3.4–13.4, p=.002) (r1). Within-family rises appear in Falcon, Flan-T5, Gemma, LLaMA-3 and Qwen2 (r2–r11, r15, r16, r20–r24).
relationships.display_finding: Each tenfold size increase is associated with 8.6 additional commonsensicality points, with a 95% confidence interval of 3.4–13.4 and p = 0.002, alongside increases within Falcon, Flan-T5, Gemma, LLaMA-3 and Qwen2.

relationships.reason: The smallest model scores highest (75.0%). 13B falls to 46.5% and 70B to 63.5%. Authors state the scaling pattern 'is not the case for LLaMA-2' (r12–r14).
relationships.display_finding: The 7B model scored highest at 75.0%, compared with 46.5% for 13B and 63.5% for 70B chat.

relationships.condition: Mistral family; Flan-T5 Large→XL; across families at similar size
relationships.reason: Mistral scores are flat or non-monotonic (80.4, 76.4, 82.3) (r17–r19), and Flan-T5-XL dips below Large (r7, r8). Authors attribute large spread at ~7B (LLaMA-2/3, Gemma, Qwen2) to training-data quantity and quality, so size alone predicts weakly (r10–r12, r15, r22).
relationships.display_finding: Mistral scores varied non-monotonically at 80.4, 76.4 and 82.3, Flan-T5-XL underperformed Large, and variation around 7B was attributed to training-data quantity and quality.
